Female Brown dottyback (Pseudochromis fuscus) attain an ultimate standard length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a size typical of small, site-attached coral reef fishes. Body mass at puberty, derived from the standard length of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters] at that milestone, is approximately 0.53 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.53 grams], reflecting the allometric relationship between linear growth and tissue accretion in this species. This modest mass at the onset of reproductive capability underscores the relatively energetic economy required for a fish that defends a small crevice territory within the reef matrix. Field surveys of this dottyback indicate that individuals begin allocating resources to gonadal development once they surpass this critical size threshold, a pattern common among pseudochromids living in structurally complex habitats where shelter availability rather than food alone limits population density.

Egg development and larval emergence in Pseudochromis fuscus proceed rapidly under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching from the demersal egg mass, is a remarkably brief 4 days [ab = 4 days]. This rapid embryogenesis is consistent with the high metabolic rates typical of small-bodied tropical marine teleosts and likely reflects selective pressures to minimize the duration of exposure to benthic egg predators such as wrasses and small moray eels. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges with an endogenous nutrient reserve that sustains it through the first critical days of exogenous feeding. Comparable developmental rates have been documented in other small pseudochromids from the Indo-Pacific, suggesting a conserved early-life strategy among members of this genus.

The wet weight at birth of the Brown dottyback is exceptionally low, measured at just 0.0013 grams [Wwb = 0.0013 grams]. This minute mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 1.35 millimeters, places the species among the smaller producers of offspring within the Pseudochromidae. Such a diminutive start necessitates a highly productive planktonic larval phase, during which the individual must grow by several orders of magnitude before it is capable of benthic settlement. The contrast between this negligible birth mass and the ultimate wet weight for females of 6.3 grams [Wwi = 6.3 grams] highlights the enormous scope for post-hatching growth. This trajectory demands efficient feeding and low mortality during the pelagic larval duration, a bottleneck that strongly influences recruitment variability in coral reef fish populations.

Reproductive output in this species, inferred from data on the congener Pseudochromis flavivertex, is impressive given the small body size of the female. Under the stable thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], individual females likely produce a single clutch of eggs approximately every 56 days [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs approximately every 56 days], with each clutch containing around 1200 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing around 1200 eggs]. This high fecundity per spawning event is characteristic of many small benthic-spawning teleosts that rely on a high initial propagule number to offset intense egg and larval predation. The combination of a moderate inter-clutch interval and a large batch size allows the species to achieve substantial annual reproductive output despite its limited body cavity and low adult biomass.

Longevity records for the Brown dottyback kept under captive conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] suggest that individuals rarely exceed a maximum lifespan of approximately six years [am = approximately six years]. This lifespan is intermediate among small coral reef fishes; some gobies and blennies live only one or two years, while certain damselfishes can persist for over a decade. The standard length at puberty of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters] is reached well within the first year of life, allowing several reproductive seasons over the course of a typical lifetime. This early onset of maturity relative to total lifespan aligns with an opportunistic life-history strategy, maximizing the number of breeding attempts before the inevitable risk of predation or senescence in a high-mortality reef environment.
